Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron in the laboratory frame. Its boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Omega$ has the outward unit normal $n$ on the relative interior of each planar face; edge and vertex values will be irrelevant under the face-area convention below. Use the SI conventions of this framework. In particular $E$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $H$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, $D$ has units $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$, $B$ has units $\mathrm T$, and a volume current density $J$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.

For the boundary integrals, let $\mathcal F$ be the finite family of relative interiors of the planar two-dimensional faces of $\Gamma$. Write $\lambda_2$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$, defined as the restriction of Lebesgue outer measure to its Carath\'eodory-measurable sets; under the assumed $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, this is a complete measure. For each face $F\in\mathcal F$, let $P_F$ be its supporting plane and fix a Euclidean isometry $\iota_F:\mathbb R^2\to P_F$. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\Gamma$ (a set in the sigma-algebra generated by the open subsets of $\Gamma$), define $dS_F(A):=\lambda_2\bigl(\iota_F^{-1}(A\cap F)\bigr)$. Any two choices of $\iota_F$ differ by an affine Euclidean isometry of $\mathbb R^2$ with absolute Jacobian determinant $1$, so the Borel change-of-variables formula makes $dS_F$ independent of that choice. Each face is bounded and lies in a finite rectangle in its plane, so $dS_F(F)<\infty$. Set $dS:=\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}dS_F$ on $\Gamma$. The edges and vertices have $dS$-measure zero and are omitted, so $n$ is the outward face normal $dS$-almost everywhere; its values on edges and vertices do not affect any boundary expression. Since $dS$ is finite and Lebesgue measure restricted to $I$ is sigma-finite, $dS\otimes d\lambda_1|_I$ is the unique sigma-finite product measure on $\Gamma\times I$, with rectangle values $dS(A)\lambda_1(J)$ for Borel $A\subseteq\Gamma$ and Lebesgue-measurable $J\subseteq I$. All boundary $L^p(\Gamma)$ and $L^p(\Gamma\times I)$ spaces and almost-everywhere statements use these measures.

Every cross product in the boundary formulas is the right-handed Euclidean cross product in the positively oriented orthonormal frame basis: for $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ and $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, $u\times v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\,u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$, as in the cross-product definition of this library.

For a real vector field $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the distribution defined by

$$\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$

As in the real graph space definition of the imported mathematical library, $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ consists of the $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional curl is represented by an $L^2$ vector field, with norm

$$\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by that imported weak-derivative convention. Let $\varepsilon,\mu:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be measurable, essentially bounded, real symmetric coefficient fields, independent of time. Require constants $0<a_\varepsilon\le b_\varepsilon<\infty$ and $0<a_\mu\le b_\mu<\infty$ such that, for almost every $x\in\Omega$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$a_\varepsilon |v|^2\le v\cdot\varepsilon(x)v\le b_\varepsilon |v|^2,\qquad a_\mu |v|^2\le v\cdot\mu(x)v\le b_\mu |v|^2.$$

The coefficient units are $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. They define bounded symmetric multiplication operators on $L^2$. Define $D(t)=\varepsilon E(t)$ and $B(t)=\mu H(t)$. The spatially varying coefficient fields are explicit local model data; they are not inferred from the homogeneous material-closure postulate. Its constant symmetric branch is a special case.

A field $E:I\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is in $C^1(I;L^2)$ when it has a derivative in the $L^2$ norm at every $t\in I$ and that derivative is norm-continuous. $C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$ means norm-continuity into the graph space. A finite-energy model solution is a pair

$$E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)),$$

with $J\in C(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, satisfying the adopted evolution equations as $L^2$ identities for each $t\in I$,

$$\varepsilon\,\partial_t E=\operatorname{curl}H-J,\qquad \mu\,\partial_t H=-\operatorname{curl}E.$$

Its stored field energy is the finite real number

$$W(t):=\frac12\int_\Omega\bigl(E(x,t)\cdot\varepsilon(x)E(x,t)+H(x,t)\cdot\mu(x)H(x,t)\bigr)\,d\lambda_3(x).$$

There are two alternative boundary models.

**PEC.** Perfect electric conductor means $E(t)\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ for every $t$, where $H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ is exactly the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ in the displayed graph norm. This closure definition is used; it is not replaced by an unproved identification with every possible trace kernel.

**Impedance.** A Green-compatible tangential boundary pair consists of measurable fields $E_\tau,H_\tau\in L^2(\Gamma\times I;\mathbb R^3)$ with $n\cdot E_\tau=n\cdot H_\tau=0$ almost everywhere and, for almost every $t$,

$$\int_\Omega\bigl(\operatorname{curl}H\cdot E-H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E\bigr)\,d\lambda_3=-\int_\Gamma n\cdot(E_\tau\times H_\tau)\,dS.$$

This Green identity is part of impedance admissibility; membership in $H(\operatorname{curl})$ alone does not assert that such an $L^2$ pair exists. Let $Y\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ be a time-independent scalar surface admittance, in siemens, with $Y\ge0$ almost everywhere. The impedance law is

$$H_\tau=Y(n\times E_\tau)\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Gamma\times I.$$

Then $Y|E_\tau|^2\in L^1(\Gamma\times I)$ and is the nonnegative outward boundary-power density in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. No pointwise boundary trace of an arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ field is asserted.

derivations.claim: The coefficient fields define bounded symmetric multiplication operators on $L^2$, so $W(t)$ is finite. For a real Hilbert-space vector $u\in C^1(I;L^2)$ and a bounded symmetric operator $M$, expand $u(t+h)=u(t)+h u'(t)+o(h)$ in the $L^2$ norm in $Q(t)=\tfrac12(u(t),Mu(t))$. Bilinearity and symmetry give $ \frac{Q(t+h)-Q(t)}h=\frac12\left(\frac{u(t+h)-u(t)}h,Mu(t+h)\right)+\frac12\left(Mu(t),\frac{u(t+h)-u(t)}h\right)\longrightarrow (u'(t),Mu(t)). $ Applying this calculation to $E,\varepsilon$ and $H,\mu$ yields $W'(t)=(\partial_tE,\varepsilon E)_{L^2}+(\partial_tH,\mu H)_{L^2}$.

Substitute the two $L^2$ evolution identities from [A1] into the derivative of step 1.1 and use symmetry of the real $L^2$ pairing: $ W'(t)=(\operatorname{curl}H,E)_{L^2}-(J,E)_{L^2}-(\operatorname{curl}E,H)_{L^2}. $ All three pairings are finite by the H(curl) and $L^2$ hypotheses and [F3].

In the PEC branch, [F2] and [A2] provide $E_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $E_n\to E(t)$ and $\operatorname{curl}E_n\to\operatorname{curl}E(t)$ in $L^2$. For every $n$, the distributional-curl definition in [F1], tested against $E_n$, gives $(\operatorname{curl}H,E_n)_{L^2}=(H,\operatorname{curl}E_n)_{L^2}$. By [F3], the left side converges to $(\operatorname{curl}H,E)_{L^2}$ and the right side to $(H,\operatorname{curl}E)_{L^2}$. Hence the first and third terms in step 2.1 cancel, and $W'(t)=-(J,E)_{L^2}$.

In the impedance branch, the Green compatibility identity in [A1] gives $(\operatorname{curl}H,E)_{L^2}-(H,\operatorname{curl}E)_{L^2}=-\int_{\partial\Omega}n\cdot(E_\tau\times H_\tau)\,dS$. The boundary law and $n\cdot E_\tau=0$ imply $ n\cdot(E_\tau\times H_\tau)=Y\,n\cdot\bigl(E_\tau\times(n\times E_\tau)\bigr)=Y|E_\tau|^2\ge0, $ since [F4] gives $E_\tau\times(n\times E_\tau)=n|E_\tau|^2-E_\tau(E_\tau\cdot n)$ and $|n|=1$. Substitution in step 2.1 gives $W'(t)=-(J,E)_{L^2}-\int_{\partial\Omega}Y|E_\tau|^2\,dS$ for almost every $t$; the boundary integrand is time-integrable by the $L^2$ trace and bounded-Y assumptions.

In either branch, $W$ is continuously differentiable by step 1.1, the volume work is integrable, and the impedance power is integrable when present. Integrating the derivative identities of steps 3.1 or 3.2 on $[s,t]\subset I$ gives exactly the two energy balances in the Statement.

For the homogeneous difference of two solutions with equal data at $t_0$, linearity gives $J=0$ and $E(t_0)=H(t_0)=0$. The coefficient lower bounds give $W(t)\ge\frac12\min(a_\varepsilon,a_\mu)(\|E(t)\|_2^2+\|H(t)\|_2^2)\ge0$. By step 4.1, $W(t)=0$ for PEC and $W(t)\le0$ for impedance whenever $t\ge t_0$; thus $W(t)=0$, and the lower bound gives $E(t)=H(t)=0$ in $L^2$ for every such $t$. This proves forward uniqueness without asserting existence.

PEC approximation uses exactly AC_omega and graph closure, with convergence of both curl and field. Impedance power uses the assumed Green identity only almost everywhere; Y>=0 and tangency give the outward sign and global L1 boundary power. C1 energy allows integration on every compact [s,t] inside I. Coercivity and nonincreasing energy prove the exact stated homogeneous zero-data forward conclusion. The opening difference language in step 5.1 is used only when that homogeneous field is itself admissible; the written Statement asserts zero-data uniqueness and does not license arbitrary subtraction of abstract Green pairs or backward uniqueness. Zero current/field, Y=0 and initial time equality pass; degenerate coefficients are excluded. Chen pp.1-5 and Beisert printed section 8.2 equations 8.3-8.9 support context, not existence or empirical validity.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite. The slice-chart definition has no manifold boundary; $S$ has no edge. If $S$ is empty, all surface functionals below are zero and the estimates are read separately without taking a supremum over the empty set.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Now $F$ is continuous on $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$. For each $x\in S$, the two one-sided limits are finite; hence there is a neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ on which $|F|$ is bounded on each side (use the defining limit with tolerance $1$ for each of $F_+(x)$ and $F_-(x)$). Away from $S$, continuity also gives a neighbourhood with a finite bound at every point. For a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, these neighbourhoods cover $K$; take a finite subcover and the maximum of its finitely many bounds. This gives a finite $M_K$ such that $|F|\le M_K$ on $K\setminus S$. Extend $F$ by zero on the null closed set $S$; the extension is measurable because the two side restrictions are continuous, and

$$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le M_K\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

The definition assumes a fixed stationary interface $S$: no time dependence of $S$ is part of the data, and the stationary jump formulas are not asserted for moving interfaces. The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. The definition is stated under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ because the surface measure it invokes is; the positivity of the surface measure of nonempty open pieces of $S$, and the finite-order estimates above, are its only uses here.

Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.

the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
(A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Fix a chart $X:V\to S$. Its coordinate tangent vectors are independent by [F2], so there are unique functions $K^a$ with $K=K^a\partial_aX$; their $C^1$ regularity is part of the stated tangent-field convention. The chart area density $J_X$ is positive and $C^1$ by [F1]. Therefore $ g_X(X(u)):=J_X(u)^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^2\partial_a(J_XK^a)(u) $ is continuous on the chart.

Let $\phi\in C^1(S)$ have compact support in this chart. By the definition of the surface gradient, $K\cdot\nabla_S\phi=K^a\partial_a(\phi\circ X)$. The surface-area formula and [F3] give $ -\int_SK\cdot\nabla_S\phi\,dS=-\int_VJ_XK^a\partial_a(\phi\circ X)\,du=\int_V\partial_a(J_XK^a)(\phi\circ X)\,du=\int_Sg_X\phi\,dS. $ Here the repeated $a$ is summed over $1,2$; compact support lets each product $J_XK^a(\phi\circ X)$ extend by zero as a $C^1$ function, and integration by parts on a rectangle containing the support has no boundary term. Thus $g_X$ from step 1.1 represents $\operatorname{Div}_S K$ on this chart.

Write the finite chart cover in [F1] as $S\cap O_j$, with each $O_j\subset\mathbb R^3$ open and contained in its chart domain. For every $x\in S$, choose one such $O_j$ and a ball around $x$ whose closure lies in $O_j$; [F4] supplies a smooth cutoff supported compactly in $O_j$ and equal to one on a smaller ball. Compactness of $S$ gives a finite subfamily of these smaller balls covering $S$. Group their cutoffs as $b_j$ by assigned chart, and let $b=\sum_jb_j$, which is positive on an open neighborhood of $S$. On that neighborhood set $\chi_j=b_j/b$. The restrictions to $S$ are smooth, sum to one, and each support is compactly contained in its assigned chart. Each $\chi_jg_j$ extends continuously by zero off its chart, so $g:=\sum_j\chi_jg_j$ is continuous on $S$. Applying step 2.1 to $\chi_j\phi$ and summing gives $ \int_Sg\phi\,dS=-\sum_j\int_SK\cdot
abla_S(\chi_j\phi)\,dS=-\int_SK\cdot
abla_S\phi\,dS, $ because $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ and $\sum_j
abla_S\chi_j=0$. By the definition of $\operatorname{Div}_S K$, $g$ is a continuous density representing it.

If $g_1,g_2$ are continuous representatives, then $\int_S(g_1-g_2)\phi\,dS=0$ for every $\phi\in C^1(S)$, hence in particular for every restriction of an ambient test in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$. Apply [F5] to $g_1-g_2$ to obtain $g_1=g_2$ pointwise on $S$. The local formula of step 1.1 is therefore independent of chart and equals the unique global representative.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] and the surface conventions of [[def-em-weak-sources]] are stated, and let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]].

Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), let $\sigma_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $K_f(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a free surface charge density in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and a tangential free surface current density in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, both stationary in $t$), and let $\rho_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$. Let $E,B,D,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$, with the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension property: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side of each field is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder, so that the fields and their first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side, locally uniformly on compact cylinders. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces.

**[Thin-interface hypothesis]** Suppose that $E,B,D,H$ satisfy the four macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] in the distributional sense on $U$ with the source pair $\rho_f=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$, $J_f=J_v+K_f\delta_S$, where the stationary-sheet pairings are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) and the equations are $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ as identities in the sense of [[def-distribution]], the fields being identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\psi$ ranging over $C_c^\infty(U)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). This thin-interface solution hypothesis is a modelling assumption of the statement: it is the natural weakening of the smooth macroscopic equations to fields with a common stationary discontinuity, and it is not deduced from the smooth-region equations alone.

Then, pointwise on $S\times I$,

$$n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f,\qquad n\cdot[B]=0,\qquad n\times[E]=0,\qquad n\times[H]=K_f,$$

with the Euclidean inner and cross products of the one-sided traces ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); equivalently $\sigma_f=n\cdot[D]$ and $K_f=n\times[H]$ recover the free sheet densities from the field jumps.

**[Weak-trace branch]** If instead of the joint extension hypothesis the fields have the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time and, in addition, the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the one-sided field traces are measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ with respect to $dS\,dt$, then the same four identities hold as identities of sheet distributions and for $dS\,dt$-almost every $(x,t)$; since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, they hold for every $x\in S$ for almost every $t$, and at every $(x,t)$ whenever the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous. Merely having one-sided spatial $C^1$ traces separately at every time does not justify the last upgrade.

**[Scope]** In the joint one-sided spacetime $C^1$ extension branch, stationarity and the joint extensions make $\partial_tD$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally integrable, contributing no delta terms. In the weak-trace branch the explicitly assumed locally integrable temporal derivatives provide this conclusion instead. No magnetic charge and no magnetic surface current are present in the sources; no dipolar sheet layer (a concentrated dipole distribution in $P$ or $M$, which would make the fields non-integrable) is included. No existence theorem for fields with singular sources is asserted, no constitutive law is used, and no empirical claim is made.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) as carried by the declared
distributional and surface source objects of [[def-em-weak-sources]]. In the
flat classical laboratory model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the positive
constants and SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], adopt the following
additional physical assumption for models using the declared point or
stationary-sheet sources: the locally integrable field pair and the
volume-plus-singular source pair of [[def-em-weak-sources]](a)-(d) must satisfy
its solution predicate (e). Explicitly,

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

are required in $\mathcal D'(U)$, meaning that all four residual pairings
defined there vanish for every compact smooth test. This is a physical adoption
of the classical vacuum idealisation in that source class, not a theorem about
sources and not a consequence of the original locally integrable source branch
of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. When the singular part vanishes, the adopted
identities coincide with that earlier weak branch.

Only source and field tuples satisfying these identities are models of this
postulate; the postulate does not assert existence for every prescribed source
pair, and compatibility conditions remain consequences to be checked. Sources
are the exact point and stationary-sheet types defined earlier, including their
properness or endpoint and tangential-current qualifications. No moving sheet,
line current, magnetic source, product of distributions, self-force,
regularisation, matter dynamics or material constitutive law is introduced.
This postulate reports no experiment or measurement and does not infer
empirical certainty from its mathematical formulation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the surface-measure interface inherited from [[def-em-surface-distribution]]
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\mathcal D'(U)$ be the space of
distributions on $U$ ([[def-distribution]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]); recall that the pairing
$\langle T,\psi\rangle$ is bilinear with no conjugation and that the
distributional partial derivatives are
$\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$
([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(a) [Fields as distributions] Locally integrable fields and source densities on
$U$ are identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

(b) [Point sources] Let $I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval,
let $z:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory whose graph map
$\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is proper into the open set $U$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$
(coulombs). By [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],

$$\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$ with
$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=0$. If instead
$I_0=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the
absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite and both endpoint
events lie in $U$, the same formulas define distributions with

$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$$

([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); a finite-history point source
therefore contributes an endpoint term unless that term is included
explicitly, and the pairings above exclude it only by the stated properness or
endpoint hypotheses.

(c) [Stationary-sheet sources] Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded
$C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side
$\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]],
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), and let
$\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous
with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$; $\sigma$ carries C m$^{-2}$ and $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$ (a tangential surface current
density; the sheet is stationary). Then

$$\langle\rho_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_S\sigma(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_SK(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$: for $\psi$ with compact support the inner
integrals are continuous in $t$ on a compact parameter interval and the
functionals are bounded by
$(\sup|\sigma\psi|)\,\mathrm{area}(S)\,\mathrm{length}$ of the time projection
of the support, and likewise in the vector case. A normal sheet current (one
with $K\cdot n\ne0$), a line current and a moving sheet are not source types of
this definition.

(d) [Unrestricted weak fields and optional interface branches] The general
field class for the solution predicate (e) consists of all locally integrable
pairs $(E,B)$ on $U$, also when the source has a stationary-sheet part. No
classical one-sided trace or off-sheet $C^1$ regularity is required to define
those four distributional pairings. Additional trace hypotheses are optional
hypotheses of interface and jump results, not admission requirements of the
general weak model.

For a pointwise classical jump branch, one may additionally assume that $E,B$
are $C^1$ off $S\times I$ and, around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side
is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of
the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. These
joint one-sided extensions make the field traces and first spatial and
temporal derivatives continuous up to that side, locally uniformly on compact
cylinders.

For the broader weak-trace branch, retain spacetime $C^1$ regularity on
$(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ and assume the original one-sided spatial
$C^1$ extensions at each time, with the explicit additional
conditions that the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the field traces are measurable and locally
integrable on $S\times I$ for $dS\,dt$. This branch supports sheet-distribution
and almost-everywhere jump identities; spatial continuity at each time gives
pointwise spatial identities for almost every time, and joint continuity of
the jump densities gives the further all-time upgrade. Separate spatial $C^1$
traces at each time alone do not imply that joint regularity or upgrade.
Whenever such traces exist, $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ denotes their jump in the chosen
normal convention.

(e) [Weak Maxwell equations with a distributional source pair] Let $E,B$ be a
field pair of class (d), let $\rho=\rho_v+\rho_s$ and $J=J_v+J_s$ be source
distributions on $U$ whose volume parts $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable
volume densities with the charge and current quantity types of
[[def-em-sources]] (the weak predicate requires this stated
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity, not the classical continuous-source
regularity) and whose singular parts $(\rho_s,J_s)$ are point sources as in (b)
or stationary-sheet sources as in (c), and let
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. Say that $E,B$ satisfy the weak Maxwell equations
with the source pair $(\rho,J)$ when, for every
$\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, the four pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish, all derivatives being distributional derivatives of the regular
distributions of the fields and the source pairings being those of (b) and (c).
This clause defines a solution predicate. When the singular parts vanish, its
four identities are the same as the locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. That earlier postulate explicitly excludes point
and sheet distributions and does not imply their physical adoption here;
adoption for the declared singular-source models is made separately, after
this definition. No physical field equation is deduced merely from defining
this predicate.

(f) [Scope] No product of two distributions is formed anywhere: the fields
occur only through their distributional derivatives paired with a test
function, and the source densities $\sigma,K$ occur only inside the ordinary
surface and time integrals of (b) and (c); products such as $\rho_sE$ or
$J_s\times B$ are not defined by this item. The definition asserts no existence
theorem for fields with singular sources, no conservation law (continuity for
these sources is proved separately where used) and no regularisation. Sources
that are not locally integrable and are not point or stationary-sheet sources,
moving sheets, line currents, and arbitrary products of distributions are
outside the definition.

Throughout, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the surface integral of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and the domains of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] are developed under that convention.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite. The slice-chart definition has no manifold boundary; $S$ has no edge. If $S$ is empty, all surface functionals below are zero and the estimates are read separately without taking a supremum over the empty set.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Now $F$ is continuous on $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$. For each $x\in S$, the two one-sided limits are finite; hence there is a neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ on which $|F|$ is bounded on each side (use the defining limit with tolerance $1$ for each of $F_+(x)$ and $F_-(x)$). Away from $S$, continuity also gives a neighbourhood with a finite bound at every point. For a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, these neighbourhoods cover $K$; take a finite subcover and the maximum of its finitely many bounds. This gives a finite $M_K$ such that $|F|\le M_K$ on $K\setminus S$. Extend $F$ by zero on the null closed set $S$; the extension is measurable because the two side restrictions are continuous, and

$$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le M_K\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

### Conventions and exclusions

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. This convention is used by the interface-derivative lemma on this page, where $\operatorname{div}F$ and $\operatorname{curl}F$ acquire the surface terms $n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\,\delta_S$; reversing $n$ reverses the signs of both sides consistently. The definition assumes a fixed stationary interface $S$: no time dependence of $S$ is part of the data, and the stationary jump formulas are not asserted for moving interfaces. The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. The definition is stated under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ because the surface measure it invokes is; the positivity of the surface measure of nonempty open pieces of $S$, and the finite-order estimates above, are its only uses here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $(S,\Omega_-,\Omega_+,n)$ be a two-sided presentation of a compact embedded $C^2$ interface in $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-em-surface-distribution]]: $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ are the two open sides and $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ is the continuous unit normal pointing from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$. Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately, with one-sided $C^1$ traces on $S$: $F$ and each first partial derivative $\partial_iF$ extend continuously from each side to $S$, and the traces $F_+,F_-\in C^0(S;\mathbb R^3)$ give the jump $[F]=F_+-F_-$.

Let $\{\partial_iF_j\}$, $\{\operatorname{div}F\}$ and $\{\operatorname{curl}F\}$ denote the locally integrable fields equal on $\Omega_\pm$ to the corresponding classical derivative of $F$; these are regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). The slice-chart definition makes $S$ a hypersurface without manifold boundary, so no edge is part of these data. Then, in the distributional sense,

$$\partial_iF_j=\{\partial_iF_j\}+n_i\,[F_j]\,\delta_S\qquad(i,j\in\{1,2,3\}),$$

and consequently

$$\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S,\qquad \operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[F]\,\delta_S,$$

as distributions on $\Omega$: their pairings agree for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$. Here $\delta_S$ is the surface distribution of [[def-em-surface-distribution]], $n\cdot[F]=\sum_i n_i[F_i]$, and $n\times[F]$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. A moving interface with $\partial_tS\ne0$ requires additional terms and is not covered; the stationary jump formulas may not be reused for a moving interface. Interfaces with a manifold boundary require separate definitions and are not included.

Assume the surface-measure convention with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the mathematical definition of the stationary surface distribution. Let $S\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface without manifold boundary, with a chosen continuous unit normal $n$ and its finite surface measure $dS$. At $x\in S$, define the tangent plane

$$T_xS:=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:v\cdot n(x)=0\}.$$

For $\phi\in C^1(S)$, meaning that its composition with each local $C^2$ surface chart is $C^1$, its surface gradient $\nabla_S\phi(x)\in T_xS$ is the unique vector satisfying

$$v\cdot\nabla_S\phi(x)=d\phi_x(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in T_xS,$$

where $d\phi_x$ is the derivative of $\phi$ in tangent directions. For a measurable tangential field $K:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\int_S|K|\,dS<\infty$, define its **weak surface divergence** $\operatorname{Div}_S K$ as the linear functional on $C^1(S)$

$$\langle\operatorname{Div}_S K,\phi\rangle:=-\int_S K\cdot\nabla_S\phi\,dS.$$

This functional is well-defined because $S$ is compact, $\nabla_S\phi$ is continuous and bounded, and $K$ is integrable. If it has a continuous density $g:S\to\mathbb R$, meaning

$$\langle\operatorname{Div}_S K,\phi\rangle=\int_S g\phi\,dS\qquad\text{for every }\phi\in C^1(S),$$

then $g$ is called a continuous representative of the weak surface divergence. The definition itself does not assert that such a representative exists or is unique; a result using pointwise $\operatorname{div}_S K$ must establish both.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $S\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface without manifold boundary, with surface measure $dS$ and a chosen unit normal. Let $K$ be a $C^1$ tangential vector field on $S$, meaning that its two coordinate components in every $C^2$ surface chart are $C^1$. Then the weak surface divergence $\operatorname{Div}_S K$ defined earlier has a unique continuous density $g:S\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$\langle\operatorname{Div}_S K,\phi\rangle=\int_Sg\phi\,dS\qquad\text{for every }\phi\in C^1(S).$$

In a chart $X:V\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to S$, write $K=K^1\partial_1X+K^2\partial_2X$ and let $J_X=\sqrt{\det(\partial_aX\cdot\partial_bX)_{a,b=1}^2}$ be its surface-area density. The representative satisfies

$$g(X(u))=J_X(u)^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^2\partial_a\bigl(J_X(u)K^a(u)\bigr).$$

This unique continuous representative is denoted $\operatorname{div}_S K$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the surface-measure interface cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact
embedded $C^2$ hypersurface whose surface measure is that of the compact
embedded $C^1$ class of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] (the $C^2$ data are
special cases of the $C^1$ data), and let $a:S\to\mathbb R$ be continuous.
Suppose that

$$\int_Sa\psi\,dS=0$$

for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]),
the pairing being the signed surface integral of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] of the continuous
function $a\,(\psi|_S)$. For complex tests the integral is defined componentwise in real and imaginary parts; the proof below uses real tests. Then $a=0$ on $S$. Equivalently, if two continuous
densities on $S$ pair equally against every test function, then they are equal
pointwise on $S$. The conclusion is pointwise and uses the continuity of $a$;
a merely locally integrable density would satisfy only an almost-everywhere
conclusion, which this statement does not claim.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and are continuous linear maps on $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ for both the weak and strong distribution topologies. These claims hold in ZF. Assuming Countable Choice for the cited Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison, if $f\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, then $\partial^\alpha u_f=u_{\partial^\alpha f}$. In particular distributional differentiation extends classical smooth differentiation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $P^m$ and $N^n$ be smooth manifolds with $m<n$, and let $F:P\to N$ be a
$C^1$ map. Then $F(P)\subseteq N$ is a null subset of $N$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
(A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Throughout, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the surface integral of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and the domains of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] are developed under that convention.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite. The slice-chart definition has no manifold boundary; $S$ has no edge. If $S$ is empty, all surface functionals below are zero and the estimates are read separately without taking a supremum over the empty set.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Now $F$ is continuous on $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$. For each $x\in S$, the two one-sided limits are finite; hence there is a neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ on which $|F|$ is bounded on each side (use the defining limit with tolerance $1$ for each of $F_+(x)$ and $F_-(x)$). Away from $S$, continuity also gives a neighbourhood with a finite bound at every point. For a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, these neighbourhoods cover $K$; take a finite subcover and the maximum of its finitely many bounds. This gives a finite $M_K$ such that $|F|\le M_K$ on $K\setminus S$. Extend $F$ by zero on the null closed set $S$; the extension is measurable because the two side restrictions are continuous, and

$$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le M_K\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

### Conventions and exclusions

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. This convention is used by the interface-derivative lemma on this page, where $\operatorname{div}F$ and $\operatorname{curl}F$ acquire the surface terms $n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\,\delta_S$; reversing $n$ reverses the signs of both sides consistently. The definition assumes a fixed stationary interface $S$: no time dependence of $S$ is part of the data, and the stationary jump formulas are not asserted for moving interfaces. The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. The definition is stated under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ because the surface measure it invokes is; the positivity of the surface measure of nonempty open pieces of $S$, and the finite-order estimates above, are its only uses here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: By [A1], $\operatorname{curl}H=J_v+K\delta_S+\partial_tD$ and $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_v+\sigma\delta_S$ hold in distributions. For any vector distribution $H$, the coordinate expression for $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}H$ is $ \partial_1\partial_2H_3-\partial_1\partial_3H_2+\partial_2\partial_3H_1-\partial_2\partial_1H_3+\partial_3\partial_1H_2-\partial_3\partial_2H_1=0, $ because distributional partial derivatives commute by [F6], so the terms cancel in pairs. Taking the divergence of the first equation and substituting the second gives the distributional source-compatibility identity $ \partial_t\rho_v+\partial_t(\sigma\delta_S)+\operatorname{div}J_v+\operatorname{div}(K\delta_S)=0. $

Let $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$ and choose a compact interval $J\subset I$ containing its time support in its interior. The function $\Phi(x,t):=\sigma(x,t)\psi(x,t)$ is $C^1$ on the compact set $S\times J$. Its time difference quotients converge uniformly in $x$ on compact subintervals to $\partial_t\Phi$, by uniform continuity of $\partial_t\Phi$; since $S$ has finite surface measure, $G(t):=\int_S\Phi(x,t)\,dS(x)$ is $C^1$ and $G'(t)=\int_S((\partial_t\sigma)\psi+\sigma\partial_t\psi)\,dS$. Also $G$ vanishes near the endpoints of $J$. Using the surface-sheet pairing and one-dimensional integration by parts [F9], $ \langle\partial_t(\sigma\delta_S),\psi\rangle=-\int_J\int_S\sigma\,\partial_t\psi\,dS\,dt=\int_J\int_S(\partial_t\sigma)\psi\,dS\,dt. $ Hence $\partial_t(\sigma\delta_S)=(\partial_t\sigma)\delta_S$, with no transport term because $S$ is fixed.

For any locally integrable scalar or vector field $f$ that is $C^1$ on the two fixed sides of $S$ and has the stated joint one-sided $C^1$ extensions, its distributional time derivative is the regular distribution of its sidewise classical derivative. Indeed, on a compact spacetime cylinder, $f=\mathbf 1_{\Omega_-}f_-+\mathbf 1_{\Omega_+}f_+$ almost everywhere because $S$ is three-dimensionally null by [F8]. Pairing with a compactly supported test $\psi$, Fubini gives $-\sum_{\pm}\int_{\Omega_\pm}\int_J f_\pm(x,t)\partial_t\psi(x,t)\,dt\,d\lambda_3(x)$. For almost every fixed $x\in\Omega_\pm$, one-dimensional integration by parts in $t$ has no endpoint term because $\psi$ is compactly supported in $I$; the joint one-sided extensions make the sidewise derivatives locally bounded near $S$, and ordinary $C^1$ regularity gives local integrability away from $S$. Fubini therefore gives $\int_U\{\partial_t f\}\psi\,d\lambda_3dt$. For complex-valued tests the same calculation is applied to real and imaginary parts. The indicators of the two sides are independent of time, so no spatial-interface delta occurs. This applies componentwise to $D,B$, and $\rho_v$.

The four spatial jumps follow from the proof argument of [A1], not by identifying its narrower published Statement with the present hypotheses. That supplier's proof applies the spatial divergence/curl jump formulas at each time, compares the volume and surface coefficients, and then localizes the continuous surface coefficients. These steps use that $S$ is fixed, that $D,B,E,H$ have the stated joint one-sided $C^1$ extensions, and that the sheet densities are continuous; they do not differentiate $\sigma$ or $K$ in time. Here $\sigma,K$ are jointly $C^1$, hence continuous and locally integrable on $S\times I$; step 1.3 supplies the same regular time-derivative premise for $D,B$. Fubini on compactly supported spacetime tests is justified by [F12]. Thus the proof-level jump argument applies to this time-dependent data, giving $n\cdot[D]=\sigma$, $n\cdot[B]=0$, $n\times[E]=0$, and $n\times[H]=K$ as surface-distribution identities. Their coefficients are continuous on $S\times I$, so the supplier's coefficient localization gives the stated pointwise identities. This is the broader consequence of its proof, not its published Statement.

The volume-current jump formula [F3] gives $\operatorname{div}J_v=\{\operatorname{div}J_v\}+n\cdot[J_v]\delta_S$. For the sheet current, pair its distributional divergence with a test $\psi$: by the distributional derivative definition and $K\cdot n=0$, $ \langle\operatorname{div}(K\delta_S),\psi\rangle=-\int_I\int_S K\cdot\nabla\psi\,dS\,dt=\int_I\langle\operatorname{Div}_S K,\psi|_S\rangle\,dt. $ The surface divergence here is the functional of [F4]; the identity uses only that $K$ is tangential and the interface has no edge. Substitution into step 1.1 yields $ \{\partial_t\rho_v+\operatorname{div}J_v\}+\bigl(\partial_t\sigma+n\cdot[J_v]\bigr)\delta_S+\operatorname{Div}_S K=0. $

By step 1.3, $\partial_t\rho_v$ is the regular distribution of a locally integrable sidewise derivative and has no $\delta_S$ term; the other volume coefficient $\{\operatorname{div}J_v\}$ is locally integrable by the one-sided $C^1$ hypotheses. In every open subset disjoint from $S$, the last two terms of step 2.2 vanish, so $\partial_t\rho_v+\{\operatorname{div}J_v\}$ pairs to zero against every compactly supported test there. By [F8] it vanishes almost everywhere on $U\setminus S$; because [F8] also gives that $S$ is three-dimensionally null, the coefficient vanishes almost everywhere on all of $U$. Removing its regular distribution from step 2.2 leaves $ \bigl(\partial_t\sigma+n\cdot[J_v]\bigr)\delta_S+\operatorname{Div}_S K=0 $ as a surface distribution.

For each $t\in I$, the field $K(\cdot,t)$ is a $C^1$ tangential field on the compact $C^2$ surface, so [F11] supplies its unique continuous weak-divergence density. In each chart this density is $J_X^{-1}\partial_a(J_XK^a)$; since $K$ is jointly $C^1$ and $J_X$ is positive and $C^1$, the chart formula is jointly continuous in $(x,t)$. Uniqueness makes these local formulas agree on overlaps. Write this joint continuous function as $g(x,t)=\operatorname{div}_S K(x,t)$. The definition [F4], integrated against temporal tests, then identifies the surface functional in step 3.1 with the spacetime distribution $g\delta_S$.

Put $q=\partial_t\sigma+n\cdot[J_v]+g$, which is continuous on $S\times I$ by the stated joint $C^1$ regularity and step 4.1. The surface-distribution identity in step 3.1 says that for every real ambient spatial test $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and real temporal test $\theta\in C_c^\infty(I;\mathbb R)$, $ \int_I\theta(t)\left(\int_Sq(x,t)\eta(x)\,dS(x)\right)dt=0. $ For fixed $\eta$, the real inner pairing $p(t):=\int_Sq(x,t)\eta(x)\,dS(x)$ is continuous in $t$ by [F10]. If $p(t_*)\ne0$, continuity gives $r>0$ with $[t_*-r,t_*+r]\subset I$ on which $p$ has the same strict sign as $p(t_*)$. Define $\theta(t)=\exp\!\left(-1/(1-((t-t_*)/r)^2)\right)$ for $|t-t_*|<r$ and $\theta(t)=0$ otherwise. This is a nonnegative smooth compactly supported temporal test, positive on that interval, so $\int_I\theta(t)p(t)\,dt$ has the same strict sign as $p(t_*)$, contradicting the displayed identity.
